Snapline 2.23.0

A capture release. Capture Area and Capture Window are now one selector — press Space to switch between dragging a region and picking a window, in either direction. Region and full-display screenshots shoot through ScreenCaptureKit, so nothing hides and settles before a shot: the Self-Timer fires the instant it hits zero and Capture Area shoots on mouse-up. Any capture in History can be brought back as a floating Quick Access card, a window shot's shadow is your call, and a pinned window shot finally looks like a window.

Capture

  • Space switches between area and window. Capture Area opens in the crosshair and Capture Window opens in window picking; Space on its own flips between them, the way the system crosshair does, in both directions. In window mode the window under the pointer lights up in Snapline's accent with its title tagged above it, and a click takes the shot. Space held during a drag still moves the selection. The crosshair appears on the hotkey itself and the camera cursor on the Space press — no mouse move needed — and the selector stays with you across a ⌘-Tab.
  • No flicker before a shot. Region and full-display screenshots capture through ScreenCaptureKit, with Snapline's own chrome left out of the frame rather than hidden first. The Capture Set pill stays up through the shots it counts, the countdown fires the instant it hits zero, and Capture Area shoots on mouse-up. The file is what it was: same pixels, same scale, same display profile.
  • The Self-Timer counts down on a window. With a sticky Self-Timer set, Capture Window picks the window first; the accent frame follows it through the countdown and the shot fires at zero. A window that closes before then cancels with a note.
  • Include Window Shadow. A new switch in Settings → General → Window captures, on by default so nothing changes unless you ask. Off, a window shot is the window alone, edge to edge, with its rounded corners transparent and no margin — for pasting into documents.
  • Smart Redact seeds the text index. With Smart Redact on capture enabled, a capture that comes back clean is searchable at once: the redaction scan's reading becomes its text index entry, instead of a second full recognition pass queued behind whatever was ahead of it. Redacted captures are indexed from the flattened file, as before, so redacted text never enters the index.

Quick Access and History

  • Show in Quick Access. Any History tile — the hover strip or the context menu — brings that capture back as a floating card, exactly as a fresh capture's would appear. It stays on top while you work in another app and survives closing the History window. It is a summon, not a capture: nothing is copied, the Editor does not open, and the card shows even with the Quick Access overlay switched off. Summoning a card that is already up brings it forward instead of doubling it.
  • The tile's hover buttons are one frosted strip in the frame's own style, sized to fit inside the Shelf's tile.
  • Cards and the Shelf stay out of each other's way. The card column steps aside for the History Shelf, opening a capture or a pin from a card puts the Shelf away, and clicks aimed at the Shelf's cells no longer land on the card column's invisible runway.

Pinned windows

  • A pinned window shot looks like a window. Its own shadow over the desktop, a hairline on the window's edge at the window's own corner radius, and the hover toolbar on the window itself — no second shadow around the margin, no border cutting through the shadow.

Fixed

  • A Recording that ended early reports "cut short" once, not twice.
  • A capture that lands in the default folder because the custom storage folder is unreachable says so on that capture, instead of the notice going to an unrelated read and the next capture filing there silently. Scrolling Capture now reports the fallback too.
  • Opening a recording from its Quick Access card no longer leaves the History Shelf floating over the Trim Editor.
  • A new recording's preview frame is generated once and shared by the card, History, the Shelf and the status menu, and a finished GIF's thumbnail is ready before its card appears.
  • The Recording overlay's key-chord capsule no longer rebuilds its text layout on every frame.

Notes

  • Screen Recording granted mid-session. Region and full-display screenshots now share Recording's behavior: a permission granted while Snapline is running takes effect after a relaunch, and the dialog says so. Capture Window works right away.
  • The History index is versioned. Fields a newer build adds now survive an older one. Versions before 2.23.0 cannot read the new file: on a downgrade, History appears empty, nothing is written, and a copy is parked beside the index as history.unreadable.json. Upgrading again restores everything; the parked copy can then be deleted.

Snapline 2.22.0

An editor release. The arrow is redrawn as Snapline's own Comet — curved with a drag, finished with an optional tail marker. Text gets a contrast outline that stays legible over anything. Every tool's options move to a row right under the toolbar, clicking selects what is actually drawn, and a shape you just drew stays live in your hands. Plus: a file deleted in Finder now takes its History entry with it.

Editor

  • The Comet arrow. A tapered ribbon that swells toward a sharp-tipped blade, in place of the stroked-line-and-triangle every markup tool draws. Drag the dot at its midpoint to curve it — drag back near straight and it snaps straight, and the bend survives moving and scaling. An optional tail marker (dot or ring, three sizes) marks the origin. The head keeps its size as you drag the arrow longer or shorter, and arrows in existing documents pick up the new look unchanged.
  • Text wears a contrast outline. A rounded halo behind the glyphs — dark ink gets a light halo, light ink a dark one — so labels stay legible over busy screenshots. It replaces the old drop shadow, and the editor shows it live as you type, exactly as it will commit. An Outline / Plain toggle per text box turns it off for quiet backgrounds, and your choice seeds the next box. Existing text annotations adopt the new look the next time a document re-renders.
  • Tool options, where your eyes are. Each tool's controls — redaction style, measure unit, text style, arrow tail, the eyedropper's copy format — now sit in a slim row directly beneath the tool buttons, beside a one-line usage hint, instead of hiding in the footer. The row is always there, so the canvas never jumps as tools change.
  • Clicking selects what is drawn. A slanted arrow or line no longer selects from the empty corners of its bounding box, a highlighter stroke selects across its whole drawn ribbon, an ellipse sheds its box corners — and deselecting by clicking empty canvas works right next to a slanted shape. The hover cursor makes the same promise the click keeps.
  • Draw, then adjust. A shape you just drew stays selected with its handles live, under whatever tool is active: grab an endpoint, the bend dot or a resize handle without a trip through the Select tool, or pick a color or style and it lands on the fresh shape directly. Counter badges work the same way.
  • Double-click places a textbox. Anywhere on the canvas, whatever tool is active — and double-click on existing text still re-opens it. Finishing by keyboard (⌘⏎, or Esc) steps back to Select, so the next click adjusts the box you committed instead of opening another one.

History

  • Deleted files leave History on their own. Delete a capture's file in Finder — or from a cleanup script, or a synced folder tidied on another machine — and its History entry leaves within about a second, instead of lingering as a missing-image tile until the next launch. A disconnected external drive is still an outage, not a deletion: its entries stay, showing placeholders until the volume returns.

Fixed

  • The buttons on the first Quick Access card after launch respond to the pointer immediately, without needing to leave the card and come back.

Snapline 2.21.0

Capture Previous Area re-shoots the last region you framed, in one action. Capture Area now drags in Snapline's own crosshair so the region can be remembered, the Editor asks before closing on unsaved work, and the Quick Access card's buttons finally say what they do.

Capture

  • Capture Previous Area. Directly under Capture Area in the status menu, and in Settings → Shortcuts (it ships unbound). It shoots the last region you framed at once — no selection pass, no countdown even with a sticky Self-Timer set — and from the menu it waits a beat for the menu to fade so it cannot land in the shot.
  • The region remembers its display. It is stored against the display it was framed on, in that display's own coordinates, so rearranging your desktop keeps it valid. When it can't be shot the same way — that display isn't connected, its resolution changed, or you haven't used Capture Area yet — the menu row dims with the reason on it, the cheat sheet says the same, and the hotkey shows a short note rather than doing nothing. Reconnect the display and the action comes back on its own.
  • Capture Area uses Snapline's own crosshair — the same selector the Self-Timer uses. The Screen Recording prompt, on a first run, now arrives before the drag rather than as it, so a framed selection is never lost to a dialog; invoking Capture Area again while the crosshair is up dismisses it. The system crosshair's extras — the magnifier loupe, Space to switch to window picking, the Option and Shift constraints — are not carried over; Space to move the selection while you drag is; Capture Window covers window picking outright.

Editor

  • Closing asks before losing work. Esc, ⌘W or the close button on a document with unsaved annotations, a crop, or Background and Combine changes now asks Save, Discard or Cancel, naming the screenshot and what would go ("2 annotations added and the crop changed"). Save runs the normal Done export and closes once the file has landed; a clean document closes at once, as before.

Quick Access card

  • The buttons say what they do. Rest the pointer on any cell and a small label names it — Pin, Convert to JPEG, Copy File, Save a copy, Convert to GIF, Clear all. A button that is refusing says why instead, and a focused button shows its tip too, so the keyboard has the same route. Tips never land in a capture or a recording.

Fixed

  • The feedback toast follows the OS theme instead of taking its tone from the desktop behind it.
  • The floating bars' glass casts a capsule-shaped shadow; the rectangular halo under the command bar over a light background is gone.

Show your clicks and keys in screen recordings

  • Highlight Clicks: every mouse click draws a brief expanding ring at the pointer — dual-tone, so it reads against any background. Display and region recordings.
  • Show Keystrokes: the keys you press appear in a capsule at the bottom of the movie, with shortcuts in the same ⌃⌥⇧⌘ symbols as the Shortcuts pane. Needs the Input Monitoring permission, asked once at the toggle; a recording never fails over it — refused access just means no capsule, and Snapline says so.
  • Both overlays are drawn into the recorded frames, so trims, GIF conversions, and shares keep them. The toggles live in the Record Screen bar and Settings → Recording, are remembered, and ship off. Worth knowing: Show Keystrokes records what you type — ordinary text included — into the video.

Snapline 2.16.0

Capture with Self-Timer: frame the region first, watch the countdown, and the shot fires by itself.

Capture

  • Capture with Self-Timer. Frame the region first, then a visible countdown runs — and the shot fires by itself. The delay is for staging: open the menu or tooltip you want inside the frame while the timer counts. Selection works exactly like a normal region capture (releasing the drag starts the timer — no extra confirm), and the countdown sits inside the region with the seconds, an Esc hint, and a ✕ to cancel. Nothing steals focus, so the menu you stage stays open, and the countdown never appears in the shot.
  • Pick 3, 5, or 10 seconds from the new status-menu item beside the Self-Timer setting — its top row remembers your last-used delay for a one-click repeat — or bind a shortcut in Settings → Shortcuts (it ships unbound). A canceled timer saves nothing and says so.
  • The invisible delay is gone. If you keep a sticky Self-Timer default set, region and main-display captures now show this same live countdown instead of silently stalling before the crosshair — same delay, visible and cancellable.

Snapline 2.15.0

History learns starred captures. The relaunch now waits for the old copy to actually exit.

History

  • History learns starred captures. Star anything worth keeping and it survives the retention sweep unconditionally — it never expires, and a starred card asks before a manual delete goes through. Star from the card's hover control or its Star/Unstar menu item; a starred capture wears a badge at rest. The History toolbar gains a Starred filter that combines with search.

Robustness

  • Fixed: Snapline could quit itself and not come back after you answered the Screen Recording prompt. The relaunch waited a fixed half-second before reopening, which could fire while the old copy was still shutting down — so nothing came back, and no crash report explained it. The relaunch now waits for the old copy to actually exit, and when it can't reopen safely it stays running and tells you instead of vanishing. The prompt for one permission no longer triggers a relaunch offer for another.
  • Also fixed: the camera bubble no longer scans for cameras on the main thread, which could stall the Record Screen bar (and probe for nearby iPhones) each time it opened; its window now closes cleanly instead of racing an in-flight animation; and the bubble's style controls no longer risk a crash from a settings change or a removed gradient stop.
